title: Embracing the future of Artificial Intelligence in the classroom: the relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking in modern education
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how education should respond to the rapid emergence of generative AI, especially large language models such as ChatGPT. The author argues that effective educational integration of AI depends on three core capacities: AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking. Rather than testing a specific K-12 literacy intervention, the paper is a conceptual discussion focused on the challenges and opportunities of AI adoption in education, especially around academic writing, classroom use, and institutional policy.

The paper uses a two-part approach: an institution-based case study at Kalaidos University of Applied Sciences in Zurich, Switzerland, combined with a narrative literature review. The case study draws on the author's teaching experience, participation in the university's AI taskforce, and informal, unstructured discussions with students and staff. A central institutional intervention described is the development of internal AI guidelines that permit but regulate student use of generative AI in written work, requiring transparency about which tools were used, why they were used, how outputs were critically evaluated, and where AI contributed to the manuscript. The paper also discusses possible classroom uses of AI, including experiments with chatbots, AI-supported case study generation, curriculum support tools, gamification, and immersive technologies.

The population and context are primarily higher education, not K-12. Participants are not formally sampled or quantified, but the text refers to students, lecturers, supervisors, and university leadership at a single Swiss university of applied sciences. The setting is mainly classroom and institutional practice in a higher-education environment, with the author explicitly noting that the discussion is focused on higher education, even if some ideas may also be relevant to children.

The main conclusion is that simply allowing or banning AI is insufficient. Institutions should cultivate an 'AI culture' through explicit guidance, workshops, AI literacy instruction, and deliberate teaching of prompt engineering and critical evaluation. The paper concludes that responsible AI integration requires not just access to tools but also educator support, institutional resources, and sustained attention to ethical and pedagogical issues. It does not provide direct experimental evidence on student literacy outcomes and is not a direct K-12 generative AI literacy effectiveness study.
quality_tier_rationale: This paper is a conceptual discussion and narrative literature review focused on higher education, not an empirical K-12 evaluation. It does not report a defined K-12 sample, intervention implementation study, comparator, validated outcome measurement, or causal design.
impact_tier_rationale: The article makes broad claims about potential relevance of AI literacy, prompt engineering, and critical thinking, but provides no direct empirical effect estimates. Impact is therefore unclear rather than demonstrated.
